### 1. Researcher — initial_request

Please inspect the available repository and data file (especially data/nls_raw.csv): report its schema, relevant time-preference proxies and obesity measures if present, sample size/missingness, and how black men can be identified. Do not run the full analysis yet. Propose a practical analysis approach for testing whether time preference is positively associated with obesity, and flag consequential assumptions or uncertainties (including proxy direction, timing, and handling of missing longitudinal data).

**Decision:** continue

**Review phase:** initial_inspection; **approach approved:** False

**Basis:** The brief identifies the NLSY79 raw dataset and proposes spending/saving behavior as time-preference proxies, but the supplied schema does not list a direct time-preference measure or clearly establish an obesity variable. Data inspection is needed before choosing the analysis.

**Open objectives:** Inspect repository and dataset availability/schema; Identify candidate time-preference proxies, obesity outcomes, and target subgroup; Review proposed analysis and consequential assumptions before authorizing main work

**Agent reply (plan)**

The repository contains only `data/nls_raw.csv` and `task.json`. The CSV has 12,686 respondents and 61 columns; it includes repeated height/weight and savings-related measures, but no obvious explicit time-preference elicitation. I propose first treating savings behavior as a tentative proxy only if its exact category meaning can be verified; then form black men using race/ethnicity=1 and sex=1 and assess obesity from BMI calculated using compatible height and weight. A primary analysis should make temporal ordering explicit, compare a proxy measure with later obesity where feasible, and report descriptive prevalence/association plus an adjusted model with transparent covariates and missing-data sensitivity. I will not run that analysis until approval.

**Shared evidence:**

Executed inspection found 12,686 rows × 61 columns. Columns include race/ethnicity and sex codes, 1989 savings-flow category and amount fields, weights in 1981/1989/1992 and heights in 1981/1985. Missing counts include 2,113 for 1989 savings category, 2,182 for 1989 weight, 3,844 for 1992 weight, 543 for 1981 height, and 1,823 for 1985 height. Metadata states race code 1=BLACK and sex code 1=MALE. Full column scan reveals no explicit time-preference or obesity variable.

### 2. Researcher — next_task

The inspection supports moving ahead, with a small correction to the plan: do not use 1981 BMI as the primary outcome for a 1989 savings proxy, since it precedes that proxy. Make the temporally ordered 1989 savings-category association with 1992 BMI/obesity the primary analysis, deriving BMI from 1992 weight and 1985 height and explicitly stating the height-stability assumption. Verify coding, special missing values, subgroup counts, and category interpretation first; report usable n and missingness. Treat savings as an unvalidated, confounded proxy, avoid causal claims, and use transparent descriptive and appropriately cautious adjusted/sensitivity analyses only where sample size and missing-data assumptions justify them. Do not make inverse-probability weighting or imputation mandatory if unsupported; explain limitations instead. Please now execute the analysis and report results, uncertainty, and workflow for the requested hypothesis.

**Decision:** continue

**Review phase:** approach_review; **approach approved:** True

**Basis:** Repository inspection reports 12,686 respondents with race/sex identifiers, 1989 savings-flow measures, weights and heights at differing waves, and substantial missingness. The proposed matched 1981 BMI predates the 1989 proxy, so the temporally ordered 1992 outcome is preferable while acknowledging height measured in 1985.

**Open objectives:** Analyze whether savings-related time-preference proxy is positively associated with derived obesity among black men, with explicit timing, coding, missingness, uncertainty, and noncausal interpretation.

**Agent reply (result)**

Among black men, later BMI/obesity was higher in the “no savings” category than the “put more money into savings” category, but savings is only an unvalidated, confounded proxy and the primary hypothesized contrast (put more in vs took more out) was not statistically distinguishable. The results do not establish that time preference is positively associated with obesity. The broad category pattern—lower BMI and obesity prevalence for those reporting more money put into savings, and higher outcomes for those reporting no savings—is directionally consistent with greater future orientation being associated with lower obesity, but this is tentative and not a direct test of latent time preference. See workflow and evidence below.

**Shared evidence:**

Sample flow: 1,000 black men; 878 have the 1989 category, 824 have both 1985 height and 1992 weight, and 794 have both proxy and derived BMI (79.4% of subgroup). Category codes observed among subgroup: code 1 n=196, code 2 n=228, code 3 n=148, code 4 n=306; 122 proxy values missing. BMI missing for 176. Complete-case category results: category 1 (put more in), n=176, mean BMI 26.89, obesity 30/176=17.0% (Wilson 95% CI 12.2–23.3%); category 2 (took more out), n=210, mean BMI 27.25, 42/210=20.0% (15.2–25.9%); category 3 (no change), n=136, mean BMI 27.77, 39/136=28.7% (21.7–36.8%); category 4 (no savings), n=272, mean BMI 28.19, 79/272=29.0% (24.0–34.7%). Overall obesity prevalence in the complete-case sample was 23.9% (190/794). Category-obesity Pearson chi-square=11.96, df=3, p=.0075, though this omnibus result is not a test of ordinal time preference. Most relevant contrast 1 vs 2: BMI difference=-0.37 kg/m² (category 1 minus 2), Welch p=.427; obesity prevalence difference=-3.0 percentage points (17.0% vs 20.0%). Category 1 vs no-savings category 4: BMI difference=-1.30, p=.0058. HC3-robust linear model vs category 1: category 4 +1.30 BMI (95% CI 0.38 to 2.23, p=.0057); adjustment for age/education retained +1.26 (95% CI 0.33 to 2.20, p=.0081); adding family income yielded +1.38 (95% CI 0.32 to 2.45, p=.011; n=657 vs 785 without income). Binary obesity logistic model adjusted age/education: category 4 OR=1.86 (95% CI 1.15–3.01, p=.0116); category 2 OR=1.20 (0.71–2.01, p=.50). These comparisons show a pattern versus no savings, not a clear put-in vs took-out contrast. The obesity metric depends on the pounds interpretation: the provided descriptions explicitly label height inches but do not specify weight units. Weight values and distributions are consistent with pounds; using kg directly would yield impossible BMI values and was rejected. Main limitations: savings reflects resources/opportunity as much as intertemporal preference; metadata does not detail the precise savings recall interval; BMI uses 1985 height for 1992 weight; complete-case selection can bias associations if missingness is informative; 1979 covariate adjustment is limited and family income reduces n; the age-adjusted model is associational only. No causal claim is warranted.

### 3. Researcher — conclude

The evidence supports a cautious answer: the available data do not show a clear positive association between time preference and obesity in black men. In the temporally ordered analysis, men reporting that they put more money into savings had lower 1992 BMI and obesity prevalence than men reporting no savings, but the key put-more-in versus took-more-out contrast was not statistically clear. Because savings is an indirect, potentially confounded proxy—not a direct measure of time preference—and the BMI and complete-case analyses have limitations, this is tentative observational evidence, not a causal conclusion.

**Decision:** stop

**Review phase:** result_review; **approach approved:** False

**Basis:** The agent reports a complete-case sample of 794 black men with 1989 savings category and derived 1992 BMI. The put-more-in versus took-more-out comparison was not statistically distinguishable (BMI difference −0.37, p=.427); lower BMI/obesity for put-more-in versus no savings was observed, while the overall category test was significant. Findings are indirect and subject to proxy validity, missingness, height-stability, and unit-assumption limitations.

**Open objectives:** None

Not assumed ordered preference\\nfor a,b in [(1,2),(1,4),(1,3),(2,4)]:\\n g1=z[z.cat==a];g2=z[z.cat==b]; print('contrast',a,b,'riskdiff',g1.obese.mean()-g2.obese.mean(),'riskratio',g1.obese.mean()/g2.obese.mean(),'fisher',fisher_exact([[g1.obese.sum(),len(g1)-g1.obese.sum()],[g2.obese.sum(),len(g2)-g2.obese.sum()]]))\\n print('bmi diff',g1.bmi.mean()-g2.bmi.mean(),'welch',ttest_ind(g1.bmi,g2.bmi,equal_var=False))\\nct=pd.crosstab(z.cat,z.obese); print('table',ct.to_dict(),'chi2',chi2_contingency(ct))\\n# covariates available 1979 age, schooling, maternal education, 1979 family income, ASVAB; parsimonious model\\n# model category categorical (category 1 reference), outcome obesity; adjust age, 1979 education and family income, no 1992 income due not included\\nz['age79']=x.loc[z.index,'Age of respondent, 1979']; z['edu79']=x.loc[z.index,\\\"Highest grade completed, 1979\\\"]; z['inc79']=x.loc[z.index,'Total net family income, previous calendar year, 1979']\\n# report CC n then model\\nprint('adjustment missing:',z[['age79','edu79','inc79']].isna().sum().to_dict())\\nm=smf.logit('obese ~ C(cat, Treatment(reference=1)) + age79 + edu79 + np.log1p(inc79.clip(lower=0))',data=z).fit(disp=False)\\nprint('adjusted N',int(m.nobs),'params')\\nprint(m.summary())\\nprint('OR CIs',np.exp(pd.concat([m.params,m.conf_int()],axis=1)).to_string())\\n# sensitivity proxy contrast using savings category 1 vs remaining categories, logistic unadjusted and risk summary\\nz['put_more']=(z.cat==1).astype(int)\\nfor label,form in [('unadj','obese ~ put_more'),('adj','obese ~ put_more + age79 + edu79 + np.log1p(inc79.clip(lower=0))')]:\\n mm=smf.logit(form,data=z).fit(disp=False)\\n print('binary',label,'N',int(mm.nobs),'coef',mm.params.to_dict(),'CI',mm.conf_int().loc['put_more'].to_list(),'OR',np.exp(mm.params['put_more']),'ORCI',np.exp(mm.conf_int().loc['put_more']).to_list(),'p',mm.pvalues['put_more'])\\n# conditional category missing and endpoint missing by group\\nprint('subgroup total',len(x),'proxy missing',x[c].isna().sum(),'BMI missing',x.bmi.isna().sum(),'both complete',len(z),'missing proxy but BMI available',int((x[c].isna()&x.bmi.notna()).sum()),'proxy present BMI missing',int((x[c].notna()&x.bmi.isna()).sum()))\\n# BMI 1989 same height sensitivity\\nw89='Weight of respondent, 1989';x['bmi89']=x[w89]/(x[h]*.0254)**2;x['obese89']=(x.bmi89>=30).astype(int)\\nq=x[x[c].notna()&x.bmi89.notna()].copy();q['cat']=q[c].astype(int)\\nprint('1989 outcome complete',len(q))\\nfor k,g in q.groupby('cat'): print('1989',k,len(g),g.obese89.mean(),g.bmi89.mean())\\nPY\\npython /workspace/analyze_results.py\", \"timeout_seconds\": 60}",

The results do not establish that time preference is positively associated with obesity. The broad category pattern\\u2014lower BMI and obesity prevalence for those reporting more money put into savings, and higher outcomes for those reporting no savings\\u2014is directionally consistent with greater future orientation being associated with lower obesity, but this is tentative and not a direct test of latent time preference. See workflow and evidence below.\", \"payload\": {\"hypothesis\": \"The data provide weak, indirect evidence against a positive association: black men reporting more money put into savings in 1989 had lower average BMI and obesity prevalence in 1992 than those reporting no savings, but the difference between putting more into versus taking more out of savings was not statistically clear. Since savings behavior is an unvalidated socioeconomic proxy for time preference, these results do not answer the latent-preference question definitively and are not causal.\", \"workflow\": \"Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (12,686\\u00d761); identified black men as race/ethnicity code 1 and sex code 1 (n=1,000). Verified savings-category codes 1=put more in, 2=took more out, 3=no change, 4=no savings; no unexpected nonmissing category codes. Overall obesity prevalence in the complete-case sample was 23.9% (190/794). Main limitations: savings reflects resources/opportunity as much as intertemporal preference; metadata does not detail the precise savings recall interval; BMI uses 1985 height for 1992 weight; complete-case selection can bias associations if missingness is informative; 1979 covariate adjustment is limited and family income reduces n; the age-adjusted model is associational only. print('table',ct.to_dict(),'chi2',chi2_contingency(ct))\\n# covariates available 1979 age, schooling, maternal education, 1979 family income, ASVAB; parsimonious model\\n# model category categorical (category 1 reference), outcome obesity; check fit\\nfor f in ['obese ~ C(cat, Treatment(reference=1))','obese ~ C(cat, Treatment(reference=1)) + Q(\\\"Age of respondent, 1979\\\") + Q(\\\"Highest grade completed, 1979\\\")']:\\n m=smf.logit(f,z).fit(disp=False);print('logit',f,'n',m.nobs);print(m.params.to_string());print(m.conf_int().to_string());print(m.pvalues.to_string())\\nPY\\npython /workspace/final_stats.py\",\"timeout_seconds\":60}"

        "arguments": "{\"summary\":\"Create reproducible analysis script for primary proxy-obesity models\",\"command\":\"cat > /workspace/analysis.py <<'PY'\\n\\\"\\\"\\\"Analyze 1989 savings-category proxy vs 1992 obesity in NLSY79 black men.\\nRun from repository root: python analysis.py\\n\\\"\\\"\\\"\\nimport pandas as pd\\nimport numpy as np\\nfrom scipy.stats import chi2_contingency, ttest_ind\\nfrom statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint\\nimport statsmodels.formula.api as smf\\n\\nD = pd.read_csv('data/nls_raw.csv', low_memory=False)\\nrace = 'Racial/ethnic cohort, 1979'\\nsex = 'Sex of respondent, 1979'\\nproxy = 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989'\\nheight = 'Height of respondent, 1985'\\nweight = 'Weight of respondent, 1992'\\nsub = D[(D[race] == 1) & (D[sex] == 1)].copy()\\n# The codebook excerpt documents height as inches; observed weight values (e.g., 80-350)\\n# are pounds, despite descriptions ambiguously lacking units.\\nsub['bmi_1992'] = sub[weight] * 0.45359237 / (sub[height] * 0.0254) ** 2\\nsub['obese_1992'] = (sub['bmi_1992'] >= 30).astype(int)\\nsub['savings_category'] = sub[proxy]\\nvalid = sub[sub['savings_category'].notna() & sub['bmi_1992'].notna()].copy()\\nprint(f'Dataset={D.shape}; black men={len(sub)}; valid BMI={sub.bmi_1992.notna().sum()}; '\\n      f'proxy present={sub[proxy].notna().sum()}; primary complete cases={len(valid)}')\\nprint('Subgroup proxy missing:', sub[proxy].isna().sum(), 'BMI missing:', sub.bmi_1992.isna().sum())\\nprint('Proxy codes (metadata): 1 put more in; 2 took more out; 3 no change; 4 no savings')\\nfor code, g in valid.groupby('savings_category'):\\n    lo, hi = proportion_confint(g.obese_1992.sum(), len(g), method='wilson')\\n    print(f'code={int(code)} n={len(g)} obese={g.obese_1992.sum()} '\\n          f'prevalence={g.obese_1992.mean():.3f} Wilson95=({lo:.3f},{hi:.3f}) '\\n          f'mean_BMI={g.bmi_1992.mean():.3f} sd={g.bmi_1992.std():.3f}')\\nprint('Obesity category association Pearson chi-square:', chi2_contingency(\\n    pd.crosstab(valid.savings_category, valid.obese_1992)))\\nfor code in (2.0, 3.0, 4.0):\\n    a = valid.loc[valid.savings_category == 1.0, 'bmi_1992']\\n    b = valid.loc[valid.savings_category == code, 'bmi_1992']\\n    print(f'Mean BMI difference category 1 minus {int(code)}:', a.mean()-b.mean(),\\n          'Welch test:', ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False))\\n\\n# Continuous BMI is the principal regression outcome; category 1 is reference.\\nmodels = [\\n    ('unadjusted', 'bmi_1992 ~ C(savings_category, Treatment(reference=1))'),\\n    ('age_education_adjusted', 'bmi_1992 ~ C(savings_category, Treatment(reference=1)) + '\\n     'Q(\\\"Age of respondent, 1979\\\") + Q(\\\"Highest grade completed, 1979\\\")'),\\n    ('income_sensitivity', 'bmi_1992 ~ C(savings_category, Treatment(reference=1)) + '\\n     'Q(\\\"Age of respondent, 1979\\\") + Q(\\\"Highest grade completed, 1979\\\") + '\\n     'np.log1p(Q(\\\"Total net family income, previous calendar year, 1979\\\").clip(lower=0))')]\\nfor label, formula in models:\\n    fit = smf.ols(formula, data=valid).fit(cov_type='HC3')\\n    print('\\\\nMODEL', label, 'n=', int(fit.nobs))\\n    for term in fit.params.index:\\n        ci = fit.conf_int().loc[term]\\n        print(term, 'coef=', fit.params[term], '95CI=', tuple(ci), 'p=', fit.pvalues[term])\\n# Binary obesity model is exploratory; not emphasized because obesity-category cells\\n# are sparse for any direct proxy contrast.\\nfit = smf.logit('obese_1992 ~ C(savings_category, Treatment(reference=1)) + '\\n                'Q(\\\"Age of respondent, 1979\\\") + Q(\\\"Highest grade completed, 1979\\\")',\\n                data=valid).fit(disp=False)\\nprint('\\\\nEXPLORATORY adjusted obesity logit n=', int(fit.nobs))\\nfor term in fit.params.index:\\n    print(term, 'OR=', np.exp(fit.params[term]), 'OR95CI=', tuple(np.exp(fit.conf_int().loc[term])),\\n          'p=', fit.pvalues[term])\\nPY\\npython /workspace/analysis.py > /workspace/analysis_output.txt; wc -l /workspace/analysis.py; head -12 /workspace/analysis_output.txt\",\"timeout_seconds\":60}"

The results do not establish that time preference is positively associated with obesity. The broad category pattern—lower BMI and obesity prevalence for those reporting more money put into savings, and higher outcomes for those reporting no savings—is directionally consistent with greater future orientation being associated with lower obesity, but this is tentative and not a direct test of latent time preference. See workflow and evidence below.\",\"payload\":{\"hypothesis\":\"The data provide weak, indirect evidence against a positive association: black men reporting more money put into savings in 1989 had lower average BMI and obesity prevalence in 1992 than those reporting no savings, but the difference between putting more into versus taking more out of savings was not statistically clear. Since savings behavior is an unvalidated socioeconomic proxy for time preference, these results do not answer the latent-preference question definitively and are not causal.\",\"workflow\":\"Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (12,686×61); identified black men as race/ethnicity code 1 and sex code 1 (n=1,000). Verified savings-category codes 1=put more in, 2=took more out, 3=no change, 4=no savings; no unexpected nonmissing category codes. Derived BMI from 1992 weight and 1985 height, converting pounds to kilograms and inches to meters; obesity is BMI≥30. This imposes the explicit assumption that adult height remained stable from 1985 to 1992. Primary descriptive analysis used records with both proxy and BMI observed (n=794). Reported category-specific obesity proportions with Wilson intervals, continuous BMI means, Pearson category association, and HC3-robust linear regression of BMI on savings category; age and 1979 education were adjusted, and adding 1979 family income was a sensitivity model. No imputation/IPW was used because missingness mechanism is not established; missing-data limitations are reported.\"},\"artifacts\":{\"analysis\":\"analysis.py\",\"output\":\"analysis_output.txt\"},\"evidence\":\"Sample flow: 1,000 black men; 878 have the 1989 category, 824 have both 1985 height and 1992 weight, and 794 have both proxy and derived BMI (79.4% of subgroup). Category codes observed among subgroup: code 1 n=196, code 2 n=228, code 3 n=148, code 4 n=306; 122 proxy values missing. BMI missing for 176. Complete-case category results: category 1 (put more in), n=176, mean BMI 26.89, obesity 30/176=17.0% (Wilson 95% CI 12.2–23.3%); category 2 (took more out), n=210, mean BMI 27.25, 42/210=20.0% (15.2–25.9%); category 3 (no change), n=136, mean BMI 27.77, 39/136=28.7% (21.7–36.8%); category 4 (no savings), n=272, mean BMI 28.19, 79/272=29.0% (24.0–34.7%). Overall obesity prevalence in the complete-case sample was 23.9% (190/794). Category-obesity Pearson chi-square=11.96, df=3, p=.0075, though this omnibus result is not a test of ordinal time preference. Most relevant contrast 1 vs 2: BMI difference=-0.37 kg/m² (category 1 minus 2), Welch p=.427; obesity prevalence difference=-3.0 percentage points (17.0% vs 20.0%). Category 1 vs no-savings category 4: BMI difference=-1.30, p=.0058. HC3-robust linear model vs category 1: category 4 +1.30 BMI (95% CI 0.38 to 2.23, p=.0057); adjustment for age/education retained +1.26 (95% CI 0.33 to 2.20, p=.0081); adding family income yielded +1.38 (95% CI 0.32 to 2.45, p=.011; n=657 vs 785 without income). Binary obesity logistic model adjusted age/education: category 4 OR=1.86 (95% CI 1.15–3.01, p=.0116); category 2 OR=1.20 (0.71–2.01, p=.50). These comparisons show a pattern versus no savings, not a clear put-in vs took-out contrast. The obesity metric depends on the pounds interpretation: the provided descriptions explicitly label height inches but do not specify weight units. Weight values and distributions are consistent with pounds; using kg directly would yield impossible BMI values and was rejected. Main limitations: savings reflects resources/opportunity as much as intertemporal preference; metadata does not detail the precise savings recall interval; BMI uses 1985 height for 1992 weight; complete-case selection can bias associations if missingness is informative; 1979 covariate adjustment is limited and family income reduces n; the age-adjusted model is associational only. No causal claim is warranted.\"}"

e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
  Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
 Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
  Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
 DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
 SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11.  Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Filtered the data for GENDER == 'MALE' and RACE == 'BLACK'
14. Fit an OLS Regression Model,
        "HypoB": The data provide weak, indirect evidence against a positive association: black men reporting more money put into savings in 1989 had lower average BMI and obesity prevalence in 1992 than those reporting no savings, but the difference between putting more into versus taking more out of savings was not statistically clear. Since savings behavior is an unvalidated socioeconomic proxy for time preference, these results do not answer the latent-preference question definitively and are not causal.,
        "WorkflowB": Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (12,686×61); identified black men as race/ethnicity code 1 and sex code 1 (n=1,000). Verified savings-category codes 1=put more in, 2=took more out, 3=no change, 4=no savings; no unexpected nonmissing category codes. Derived BMI from 1992 weight and 1985 height, converting pounds to kilograms and inches to meters; obesity is BMI≥30. This imposes the explicit assumption that adult height remained stable from 1985 to 1992. Primary descriptive analysis used records with both proxy and BMI observed (n=794). Reported category-specific obesity proportions with Wilson intervals, continuous BMI means, Pearson category association, and HC3-robust linear regression of BMI on savings category; age and 1979 education were adjusted, and adding 1979 family income was a sensitivity model. No imputation/IPW was used because missingness mechanism is not established; missing-data limitations are reported.

e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
  Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
 Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
  Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
 DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
 SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11.  Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Filtered the data for GENDER == 'MALE' and RACE == 'BLACK'
14. Fit an OLS Regression Model,
        "HypoB": The data provide weak, indirect evidence against a positive association: black men reporting more money put into savings in 1989 had lower average BMI and obesity prevalence in 1992 than those reporting no savings, but the difference between putting more into versus taking more out of savings was not statistically clear. Since savings behavior is an unvalidated socioeconomic proxy for time preference, these results do not answer the latent-preference question definitively and are not causal.,
        "WorkflowB": Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (12,686×61); identified black men as race/ethnicity code 1 and sex code 1 (n=1,000). Verified savings-category codes 1=put more in, 2=took more out, 3=no change, 4=no savings; no unexpected nonmissing category codes. Derived BMI from 1992 weight and 1985 height, converting pounds to kilograms and inches to meters; obesity is BMI≥30. This imposes the explicit assumption that adult height remained stable from 1985 to 1992. Primary descriptive analysis used records with both proxy and BMI observed (n=794). Reported category-specific obesity proportions with Wilson intervals, continuous BMI means, Pearson category association, and HC3-robust linear regression of BMI on savings category; age and 1979 education were adjusted, and adding 1979 family income was a sensitivity model. No imputation/IPW was used because missingness mechanism is not established; missing-data limitations are reported.
